title: The Inquisition
hook: converts are watched and tried; some keep Judaism in secret

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shtetl: mud, a market square, candles on Friday. Your line was the little town. Did you find a town's name in your family? Today, the end of the week, and candles of a very different kind, lit in secret, far to the west. Day nine hundred forty-five.

Friday evening in a Spanish city. A family that has been Christian on paper for years sits down to dinner. Before sunset the mother has changed the tablecloth and put on clean linen. Somewhere out of sight, perhaps inside a jar, perhaps in a cellar, a small lamp is burning. Nobody says why. Across the street, a neighbor notices the clean linen and the smokeless chimney on Saturday. That neighbor may soon be asked to tell what they saw. Today, the conversos, and the Inquisition that watched them.
screen: `FRIDAY IN A SPANISH CITY.` → `A LAMP IN A JAR.` → `A NEIGHBOR WATCHING.`

segments.voice: We return to Spain, where we left it with the riots. In those riots and the years that followed, Jews converted to Christianity, some under threat of death, some under pressure, some by their own choice. In Spanish they were called conversos, converts, or New Christians. Some became devoted Catholics. Some kept parts of Jewish life in secret. Others lived somewhere in between. Hebrew sources call those forced into baptism anusim, the ones who were compelled. Suspicion fell on conversos as a group. The Spanish Inquisition was a tribunal set up under the Spanish crown, with the pope's approval, to root out heresy among the baptized. That detail matters: it had authority over Christians, so in its early years its chief target was the converso, the Christian suspected of still being a Jew. The Inquisition published lists of signs to watch for: lighting candles on Friday night, changing into clean clothes for the Sabbath, refusing pork, fasting on the Day of Atonement, washing a body for burial in the Jewish way. Neighbors and servants were invited to come forward. Trials followed, with property seized, families shamed, and some of the accused burned. Sincere Christians were caught up too, because a family's past was enough to make it suspect. So what was hidden faith? Sometimes a few customs kept up without words. A grandmother's habit of lighting a candle out of sight. A prayer whispered in a mixture of languages. Tradition says some families kept such customs for generations, long after anyone remembered the reason. This week has followed Jews out of England, through the plague years, into Poland and its little towns, through Yiddish and Glückel's pages. It ends here, with faith kept behind a closed door.
screen: `CONVERSOS: NEW CHRISTIANS.` · `A TRIBUNAL FOR THE BAPTIZED.` · `LISTS OF SIGNS TO WATCH FOR.` · then, large: `FAITH BEHIND A CLOSED DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: honor hidden faith. Let your breath settle. Think of the people, in every age and every tradition, who have had to keep what they believed out of sight. Picture one of them: a mother in Spain changing the tablecloth on a Friday, someone keeping a fast at a work lunch without a word, a person reading scripture on a phone under a desk. You don't need words. Just keep them company for a moment. If you pray, you can remember them in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Converso. A Jew who became a Christian in Spain or Portugal, by force, pressure or choice, and who could be watched, accused and tried for keeping Jewish ways. Today's word.
Your line: hidden faith. Today, if you see someone keeping a quiet custom, a grace before eating, a fast, a head covering, give it room without comment. Day nine hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Jewish communities remember the anusim, the forced converts, in study and storytelling, and some descendants of conversos today are exploring and reclaiming their Jewish roots.
